How Blockchains and Digital Assets Really Work

Start with the machinery: what a shared ledger is, how hashes and blocks make records tamper-evident, and how Bitcoin, Ethereum and smart contracts build on that idea. Then look honestly at the different kinds of digital assets and at where the technology helps, and fails, in African settings.
How a blockchain keeps a shared record: ledgers, hashes, blocks and nodes

A **ledger** is simply a record of who owns what and who paid whom. Your bank keeps a ledger of your account. An ajo or esusu group keeps one in a notebook held by the treasurer. In both cases everyone trusts **one keeper**. If the keeper makes a mistake, loses the book or cheats, the members have a problem.
A closed ledger book
A blockchain is a ledger, a record of payments and ownership, kept in many copies instead of one.

A **blockchain** is a ledger that is copied onto many computers at once, called **nodes**. There is no single keeper. Every node holds the full history, checks new entries against agreed rules, and updates its copy. Because there are thousands of copies, nobody can quietly change the record on their own. This idea was first used at scale by Bitcoin, which started running in January 2009.
Hashes: a fingerprint for data

The tool that makes this work is the **hash function**. A hash function takes any data, a word, a page or a whole block of payments, and produces a short fixed-length code called a **hash**. Bitcoin uses a hash function called **SHA-256**. Three properties matter. The same input always gives the same hash. Changing even one letter or one digit gives a completely different hash. And you cannot work backwards from the hash to the original data. So a hash works like a fingerprint: it identifies the data without revealing it, and any change shows up immediately.
Blocks linked into a chain

New payments are collected into a **block**. Each block stores its list of transactions, a time stamp, and the hash of the block before it. That last item is the clever part. Because every block carries the fingerprint of the previous block, the blocks form a chain. If someone edits an old block, its hash changes, the next block no longer matches it, and every block after that is broken too.

Worked example: how a hash chain exposes tampering

For example, imagine a group of five traders, led by Amaka, who each keep a copy of a simple chained record of their weekly contributions. The hashes below are shortened and made up for teaching; real ones are 64 characters long.
Block 1 records: Amaka paid 5,000 naira, Bola paid 5,000 naira. Its hash is 7F3A.
Block 2 records two more payments and also stores 7F3A, the hash of Block 1. Its own hash is C91E.
Bola secretly edits his copy of Block 1 so it says he paid 50,000 naira. When his software recalculates, Block 1 now hashes to 2B88, not 7F3A.
Block 2 in Bola's copy still says the previous hash is 7F3A, so his chain no longer links. To hide the edit he would have to recalculate every later block.
Even if he did, the other four copies still show 7F3A. Four honest copies outnumber one altered copy, so the network rejects his version.
The edit is not impossible, but it is visible at once and is outvoted. That is what people mean by a tamper-evident or tamper-resistant record.
Agreeing on the next block

Because there is no keeper, the nodes need a rule for deciding which new block is accepted. This rule is called **consensus**. Bitcoin uses proof of work and Ethereum now uses proof of stake; you will meet both in the next lesson. For now, remember that consensus is what replaces the trusted treasurer: the rules, enforced by many computers, decide.

Tamper-evident does not mean true

A blockchain only proves that a record has not been changed since it was written. If false information is entered, for example a fake delivery record, the blockchain will faithfully keep the false record forever. And because payments cannot be reversed, a mistake or a scam payment usually cannot be undone.
Public and private blockchains

Bitcoin and Ethereum are **public** or **permissionless**: anyone can run a node, read the record and send transactions. Some companies and governments use **private** or **permissioned** blockchains, where only approved organisations run nodes. Private chains can be faster and keep data confidential, but you are back to trusting a small group, so always ask who controls the nodes.

Finally, public blockchains are **pseudonymous**, not anonymous. Your name is not written on the chain, but every payment from an address is visible forever. Once an address is linked to you, for example through an exchange that verified your identity, your whole history can be read.

**Bitcoin** was described in a 2008 paper published under the name Satoshi Nakamoto, and the network started in January 2009. It does one main job: it moves and records a digital currency, bitcoin (BTC), without a bank. Its rules cap the total supply at **21 million bitcoin**, and a new block is added roughly every **10 minutes**. That fixed supply is one reason some people treat it as a store of value, but its price still swings sharply.
A person standing beside a large bitcoin symbol
Bitcoin was the first blockchain in wide use, built to move one digital currency without a bank.
Consensus: proof of work and proof of stake

In **proof of work**, used by Bitcoin, computers called **miners** compete to solve a hard guessing puzzle using hashes. The winner adds the next block and earns newly created bitcoin plus fees. Cheating would mean out-computing most of the network, which is extremely costly. The downside is very high electricity use.

In **proof of stake**, used by Ethereum since an upgrade called **The Merge** in September 2022, **validators** lock up (stake) their own ether as a deposit. Validators are chosen to propose and confirm blocks, and a validator who breaks the rules can lose part of the deposit. Ethereum reports that the switch cut its energy use by more than 99%.

Ethereum and smart contracts

**Ethereum** is a blockchain designed to run programs, not only payments. These programs are called **smart contracts**: code stored on the blockchain that runs exactly as written when someone sends it a transaction. Smart contracts are used to create new tokens, run lending and trading services without a company in the middle (often called **DeFi**, decentralised finance), and issue **NFTs**, tokens that record ownership of a unique item.

Every action on Ethereum costs a fee called **gas**, paid in ether (ETH). Each operation uses a set number of gas units, and the user offers a price per unit, usually quoted in **gwei**. One gwei is one billionth of an ETH. A simple ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas units; smart contract actions use more.
Worked example: working out a gas fee
For example, Chioma wants to send some ETH to her sister. Her wallet shows a gas price of 20 gwei at that moment. Gas prices change minute by minute, so this figure is only for practice.
Gas used for a simple ETH transfer: 21,000 units.
Fee in gwei: 21,000 x 20 = 420,000 gwei.
Convert to ETH: 420,000 divided by 1,000,000,000 = 0.00042 ETH.
If a token swap through a smart contract used 150,000 gas at the same price, the fee would be 150,000 x 20 = 3,000,000 gwei = 0.003 ETH, about seven times more.
The fee for the simple transfer is 0.00042 ETH. Smart contract actions cost more because they do more work, and fees rise when the network is busy.

Smart contracts are not smart, and not legal contracts

A smart contract does exactly what its code says, including any mistakes. In 2016 a flaw in an Ethereum project called The DAO let an attacker drain a large share of its funds. A smart contract also cannot see the outside world on its own: it cannot know whether goods arrived unless someone feeds it that information. That outside data source is called an oracle, and it is often the weak point.

Ethereum is not the only smart contract blockchain. Others, such as BNB Chain, Solana and Tron, run similar programs, often with lower fees, and many stablecoin transfers happen on these cheaper networks. There are also **layer 2** networks, such as Arbitrum and Optimism, which bundle many transactions together and then record the result on Ethereum to cut costs. This is why a wallet or exchange will ask you to choose a **network** before you send anything.

Keep the two layers separate in your mind. The **blockchain** is the shared record. **Coins and tokens** are assets recorded on it. Bitcoin's coin is BTC; Ethereum's coin is ETH; thousands of other tokens live on Ethereum and similar chains. When someone says 'crypto' they may mean any of these, so ask which one.

Remittances: the most-cited African use

Families across Africa receive money from relatives abroad, and traditional transfers can be expensive. Stablecoins are often promoted as a cheaper route: the sender buys dollar tokens, sends them across a blockchain in minutes, and the receiver sells them for naira. Whether that is really cheaper depends on every step, so do the arithmetic.
A person sending money from a phone
Cross-border transfers are the use case most often promoted in Africa, so cost every step before believing the claim.
Worked example: costing a 200 dollar transfer two ways
For example, Ifeoma's brother in the UK wants to send her the equivalent of 200 US dollars. The fees below are assumptions for practice, not real quotes from any company.
Route A, a traditional transfer: a 10 dollar fee plus an exchange-rate margin of 3%. Margin: 3% of 200 = 6 dollars. Total cost: 10 + 6 = 16 dollars, which is 8% of the amount.
Route B, stablecoin: a 1% fee to buy the tokens = 2 dollars, leaving 198. A network fee of about 1 dollar leaves 197.
Ifeoma sells 197 dollars of tokens to a buyer in Nigeria at a rate 2% worse than the market: 2% of 197 = 3.94 dollars.
Total cost of Route B: 2 + 1 + 3.94 = 6.94 dollars, about 3.5% of 200.
Now add the risks Route B carries: the buyer may pay with a fake alert or stolen funds, her bank may question the payment, and a wrong address or network loses everything.
On paper Route B costs about 6.94 dollars against 16, but only if every step is done safely and legally. A regulated transfer app with a good rate may close much of the gap with far less risk.
Stablecoins and the search for dollars

Many Nigerians use dollar stablecoins to protect savings from naira inflation. This is a real need, but a stablecoin is only as good as its issuer. The issuer can freeze tokens, and reserves may not be what is claimed. In May 2022 an algorithmic stablecoin called TerraUSD, which relied on a formula rather than cash reserves, lost its dollar value within days, and holders lost most of their money.
The eNaira

The **eNaira** was launched on 25 October 2021. It is a central bank digital currency: a digital form of the naira issued and regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria. It is not a cryptocurrency, because one central authority controls it, and adoption has been low. It shows that 'digital money' and 'blockchain' are not the same as 'decentralised'.
Rules in Nigeria keep changing

In February 2021 the Central Bank of Nigeria directed financial institutions to stop processing cryptocurrency transactions. In March 2025 the Investments and Securities Act 2025 was signed, recognising digital assets as securities and bringing them under the oversight of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC Nigeria). Rules and enforcement have continued to change, so always check current announcements on the CBN and SEC Nigeria websites before acting.

When you hear any new 'blockchain for Africa' claim, ask three quick questions. What does it replace, and how much does the current option really cost? Who pays the fees and who earns from them? Is there evidence of real users today, or only plans and pilot announcements? Projects that cannot answer these are ideas, not solutions.
Honest limits
**Garbage in, garbage out**: a supply-chain or land-record blockchain is only as true as the person typing the data.
**Irreversibility**: there is no customer care to reverse a mistake or a fraud.
**Access**: users still need smartphones, data, and naira on-ramps such as banks or agents.
**Regulation and tax**: the legal position can change quickly.
**A simpler tool often works**: a shared spreadsheet or a regulated payment app may solve the same problem more cheaply.

Coins do not sit inside your phone. They are entries on the blockchain. What a wallet actually stores is your **private key**, the secret that lets you sign a payment from your address. Your **address** is public, like an account number. Your private key is like the PIN, password and signature together, and anyone who has it can take everything.
A closed padlock with a key
Whoever holds the key controls the coins; the wallet app is only the lock box.

Most wallets create your keys from a **recovery phrase** (also called a seed phrase), usually **12 or 24 ordinary English words** in a fixed order. If your phone is lost, typing those words into a new wallet restores everything. That also means the phrase is the most valuable thing you own in crypto. A stranger with your 12 words does not need your phone, your PIN or your face.

Whichever wallet you use, the phone itself must be clean. Install apps only from the official Google Play Store or Apple App Store, never from APK files shared on WhatsApp or Telegram. Keep the phone's software updated, use a screen lock, and do not root or jailbreak a phone that holds keys. Watch your transaction history too: in a trick called **address poisoning**, scammers send a tiny amount from an address that looks almost the same as one you use, hoping you will later copy the wrong one from your history. Always copy addresses from the original source, not from past transactions.
A simple rule for amounts: while you are learning, keep only what you are prepared to lose completely in any hot wallet or exchange account.

Worked example: a test transaction before the real one

For example, Bisi has 50 USDT on an exchange and wants to move it to her new mobile wallet. The exchange charges a withdrawal fee of 1 USDT (an assumption for practice; fees differ by platform and network).
She checks that the exchange withdrawal network matches the network her wallet address is on. The same token can exist on several networks, and sending on the wrong one can lose it.
She copies her wallet address and compares the first six and last six characters on both screens, because some malware swaps copied addresses.
She withdraws 5 USDT as a test. After the 1 USDT fee, 4 USDT arrives. She confirms it on her wallet and on a block explorer.
She sends the remaining 45 USDT. After another 1 USDT fee, 44 USDT arrives.
Total received: 4 + 44 = 48 USDT. Total fees: 2 USDT, which is 4% of 50.
The test cost her an extra 1 USDT but proved the address and network were right before she risked the rest. On small amounts fees bite hard, so she plans fewer, larger transfers in future.

One last habit: plan for your family. If something happens to you, could anyone you trust find and use your assets? Write simple instructions on where your records are kept, without writing the phrase itself in the same place.

Most people who lose money in crypto never researched what they bought. They saw a screenshot of profits or heard a friend's tip. Due diligence means checking a claim before you believe it or repeat it. The same six steps work for a famous coin, a new token, or a company pitching a blockchain product to your employer.

Follow the steps in order and write notes at each one, so your verdict rests on evidence rather than excitement.
The six steps in practice
**Write down the claim** in one sentence: for example 'This token lets farmers get paid faster.' Note who is making the claim and whether they gain if you believe it.
**Read primary documents**: the project's official website, whitepaper and documentation. Can you say what problem it solves and why it needs a blockchain at all?
**Check team and money**: are the founders named and real? Who funded it? How many tokens do insiders own, and when can they sell?
**Verify on-chain**: use a block explorer to confirm the contract address, the number of holders and whether a few wallets own most of the supply.
**Check regulator notices**: search the SEC Nigeria website for warnings or registration, and look for alerts from regulators abroad.
**Write a balanced verdict**: real potential, real limits, open questions, and a clear statement that it is not investment advice.
Reading tokenomics

**Tokenomics** describes how many tokens exist and who gets them. Three numbers matter. **Circulating supply** is how many tokens can be traded today. **Total supply** is how many exist or will exist. **Unlock schedule** says when locked tokens, often held by the team and early investors, can be sold. **Market capitalisation** is price x circulating supply. **Fully diluted value** is price x total supply.
Worked example: what an unlock does to the numbers

For example, Halima is asked by a colleague about a new token. To practise, we use an invented token called SampleToken with simple numbers: total supply 1,000,000,000 tokens, 150,000,000 circulating, price 0.10 dollars. Team and early investors hold 400,000,000 tokens that unlock in 12 months.
Market capitalisation today: 150,000,000 x 0.10 = 15,000,000 dollars.
Fully diluted value: 1,000,000,000 x 0.10 = 100,000,000 dollars, almost seven times larger.
After the unlock, circulating supply becomes 150,000,000 + 400,000,000 = 550,000,000 tokens.
If buyers' total demand stays at 15,000,000 dollars, the price that supports it is 15,000,000 divided by 550,000,000 = about 0.027 dollars.
That is a fall from 0.10 to 0.027, roughly 73%, without anything else going wrong.

A small circulating supply with a big unlock ahead is a warning sign. Halima writes that insiders may sell into the market and that the token's low 'market cap' hides a much larger fully diluted value.

While reading the documents, look for an independent **security audit** of the smart contracts, published by a named auditing firm, and read its list of unresolved issues. Treat these as warning signs: a whitepaper that talks mostly about price and profits, promised returns of any fixed percentage, founders who are anonymous or use cartoon avatars, and a token that has no clear use except being bought and sold.
Using a block explorer

Every public blockchain has free **block explorers**, websites where you paste an address or a transaction hash (its ID) and see the record. Etherscan is widely used for Ethereum, and mempool.space for Bitcoin. Check that a payment someone claims to have sent actually exists and has confirmations, that the token contract address matches the one on the official website, and how much of the supply sits in the top 10 wallets.

Know the recovery arithmetic

Losses and gains are not symmetrical. If an asset falls 50%, it must then rise 100% just to get back to where it started. A 90% fall needs a 900% rise. Write this on your research notes so headline gains do not hide the downside.

Worked example: testing a 40% monthly promise
For example, Grace is added to a Telegram group promising '40% every month from our AI crypto trading robot'. She has 200,000 naira and decides to check the maths before anything else.
Compounding for 12 months means multiplying by 1.4 twelve times. 1.4 squared is 1.96; to the 4th power is about 3.84; to the 8th about 14.76; to the 12th about 14.76 x 3.84 = 56.7.
After one year: 200,000 x 56.7 = about 11,340,000 naira.
If this were real, a small sum would become millions in a few years, and anyone running it would not need her 200,000 naira.
She also notices the group admin will not name the company, and members post only screenshots, never block explorer links.
The promise multiplies money about 57 times a year, which no honest business delivers. Grace leaves the group and warns the friend who added her.
If you have shared your phrase or signed a bad approval

Act in this order. 1) On a clean device, create a brand-new wallet with a new phrase and move any remaining funds into it at once. 2) If you signed a token approval, revoke it with the explorer's token approval checker or a revoke tool such as Revoke.cash. 3) Change exchange passwords and two-factor settings. 4) Then record evidence and report.
Safer person-to-person (P2P) trades

Many Nigerians buy and sell crypto directly with other people, often through an exchange's P2P marketplace. The platform usually holds the seller's crypto in **escrow** until the seller confirms payment. The danger is confirming too early. Open your own bank app and check that the naira has actually landed; never rely on an SMS alert or a screenshot, both of which are easy to fake. Check that the sender's name matches the buyer's verified name, refuse payments from third parties, and keep every conversation inside the platform's chat so there is a record if you need to raise a dispute.

Report to the exchange you sent from; exchanges can sometimes flag or freeze funds that reach their own platforms.
If naira moved through a bank or payment app, report to that bank or app immediately.
Report to the police or the EFCC, and report unregistered investment schemes to SEC Nigeria.
Warn your group or family so the scam does not spread.
Beware the second scam: 'fund recovery'

Victims are often contacted by 'hackers', 'recovery agents' or fake lawyers who promise to trace and return stolen crypto for an upfront fee. These are scams too. Genuine reporting to banks, exchanges and law enforcement does not require you to pay a stranger in crypto.

Prevention is far cheaper than recovery. Keep a short rule list on your phone: never share the phrase, never sign what you do not understand, never pay to withdraw, never release crypto before money is confirmed, and always verify through a channel you found yourself.
Anyone asking for your recovery phrase is a thief, whatever they call themselves.
A fee to withdraw your 'profits' means the profits were never real.

The five-question blockchain test

A blockchain is slower and more complex than an ordinary database. It earns its place only when several conditions are true together. Work through these five questions with the person. If most answers are 'no', a simpler tool is almost always better.
Does it need a blockchain?
Several parties share records
Parties do not trust each other
No acceptable trusted middleman
Tamper-evidence really matters
Data enters accurately
Only when most boxes are ticked does a blockchain beat a shared database or spreadsheet.
Worked example: a cooperative asks for 'a blockchain ajo'

For example, Folake chairs a women's thrift cooperative in Ibadan with 30 members who each contribute 10,000 naira weekly. A vendor has offered to build them 'a blockchain savings app'. She asks for your view.
Size the problem: 30 x 10,000 = 300,000 naira collected every week, about 1,200,000 naira in a four-week month.
Ask the real problem: members complain they cannot see the records between meetings and worry about the treasurer's notebook.

Run the five questions: several parties share records (yes); they distrust each other (partly); no trusted middleman (no, they have an elected treasurer and a bank); tamper-evidence matters (somewhat); data enters accurately (only if the treasurer types it correctly, the same as now).
Notice that the vendor's app would still depend on the treasurer entering payments, and members would need data and a new app.
Suggest a simpler fix: a cooperative bank account needing two signatories, a shared view-only spreadsheet updated weekly, and a monthly bank statement posted in the WhatsApp group.

Two of five answers are clearly 'yes'. Your recommendation: the transparency problem is real, but a two-signatory account plus a shared record solves it today at almost no cost. Revisit blockchain only if those fail.
Questions to put to a vendor
When a company pitches a blockchain product to your organisation, ask for written answers to these questions before any money is committed. Vague or evasive answers are themselves a finding.
Is it a public blockchain or a private one, and who exactly runs the nodes?
Who enters the data, and what stops a wrong or false entry?
What does it cost in total each year, including transaction fees, hosting and support?
Does it involve a token? If so, why is a token needed, and who holds most of it?
Has the code been reviewed by an independent security auditor, and can we see the report?
If your company closes, can we still get our records out in a usable form?

Write your findings as a short note with four headings: the problem, the proposed solution, the five-question test results, and your recommendation with a simpler alternative. A written note is easier for a committee to discuss than a verbal opinion, and it shows you judged the idea on evidence.

When a friend asks 'should I buy this coin?', move the conversation from the coin to her situation. Does she have savings for emergencies? Any loan with high interest? You can say clearly: 'I can show you how to check it, but I can't tell you whether to buy.'

Do not collect money from others to 'invest for them', do not share your own trades as tips, and do not promise anyone returns. Even with good intentions, this can make you responsible for their losses and may need a licence.
It is also fine to say 'I don't know.' A literate person knows where her knowledge ends. Offer to look it up, using the six-step workflow from Module 2, and come back with a written note.

The rules, in general terms

In Nigeria, the **Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC Nigeria)** regulates investments and securities, and the Investments and Securities Act 2025 brings digital assets under that framework. In practice, operating a platform, managing other people's money or giving investment advice as a business may require registration. The **Central Bank of Nigeria** sets rules for banks and payments. Details change, so check the SEC Nigeria and CBN websites for current rules rather than relying on social media, and take advice from a qualified professional if you plan anything beyond education.
**Disclose interests**: if you own an asset you mention, say so.
**No paid promotion**: do not accept money or free tokens to promote a project to your network.
**No signals groups**: running 'buy now' alert groups is advice, and often a pump-and-dump tool.
**Add a clear line**: 'This is education, not investment advice' on slides, handouts and notes.

Sponsors need the same care. If an exchange or crypto company offers to pay for your workshop, you must tell participants who the sponsor is, and you must keep control of the content, including scam warnings and the risks of the sponsor's own type of service. If the sponsor wants you to promote sign-ups or a token, decline the sponsorship.

How a blockchain really works, and where it fails
How a blockchain really works, and where it fails.
This is the video for module 1 of Blockchain and Digital Assets Literacy.
Why this matters
A record with no single keeper
A ledger records who paid whom
Usually we trust one keeper
A blockchain copies it to many computers
Know how it works before you trust it
A ledger is simply a record of who owns what and who paid whom. Your ajo or esusu treasurer keeps one in a notebook.
Everyone trusts one keeper. If she makes a mistake, loses the book or cheats, the members have a problem.
A blockchain is a ledger copied onto many computers at once, called nodes. There is no single keeper.
In this video you will see how it works, and its honest limits.
Step by step
Tamper-evident does not mean true.
The payment is broadcast
Nodes check it against the rules
Payments are grouped into a block
The block is linked by its hash
Every copy is updated
Step 1. A payment is sent out to the network.
Step 2. Many independent computers check it against the agreed rules.
Step 3. Payments are grouped into a block, with a time stamp.
Step 4. The block stores the hash of the block before it. A hash is a short code, like a fingerprint for data. Change one letter, and the hash changes completely.
Because each block carries the fingerprint of the one before, the blocks form a chain.
Step 5. Every copy is updated. The rule that decides which block is accepted is called consensus. It replaces the trusted treasurer.
But remember. A blockchain only proves a record was not changed. If false information goes in, it keeps that false record forever.
Worked example
How the chain exposes cheating
Block 1: Amaka and Bola pay 5,000 each
Block 2 stores Block 1's fingerprint
Bola edits his copy to 50,000
His fingerprint changes; the chain breaks
4 honest copies outvote 1 altered copy
For example, five traders led by Amaka each keep a copy of a chained record of their weekly contributions.
Block 1 records that Amaka paid 5,000 naira and Bola paid 5,000 naira.
Block 2 records two more payments, and also stores the fingerprint of Block 1.
Bola secretly edits his copy of Block 1 to say he paid 50,000 naira.
Now Block 1 has a new fingerprint, and Block 2 no longer links to it.
The other four copies still match each other, so the network rejects his version. The edit is visible at once, and outvoted.
Know the difference
Bank ledger and public blockchain
The bank keeps the record
Payments can often be reversed
Customer care fixes mistakes
Linked to your BVN and name
Thousands of nodes keep it
Confirmed payments are final
Wrong address: money usually lost
Pseudonymous, not anonymous
With a bank, one company keeps the record. A payment can often be reversed through a dispute, and customer care fixes mistakes.
On a public blockchain, confirmed payments are final. Nobody fixes a mistake. A wrong address usually means the money is lost.
And it is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Once an address is linked to you, your whole history can be read.
Agreeing on blocks
Proof of work and proof of stake
Winner solves a hash puzzle
Supply capped at 21 million
Cheating costs their deposit
Used by Ethereum since 2022
Runs smart contracts
Bitcoin uses proof of work. Computers called miners compete to solve a hash puzzle, using a lot of electricity. A new block comes roughly every 10 minutes, and supply is capped at 21 million bitcoin.
Ethereum has used proof of stake since September 2022. Validators lock up their own ether as a deposit, and lose part of it if they cheat.
Ethereum also runs smart contracts: code that runs exactly as written, mistakes included.
Name the category
Not all crypto is the same
eNaira: central bank money, not crypto
Stablecoins: only as good as the issuer
Established crypto: BTC, ETH, big swings
NFTs: little resale demand, fakes
New tokens and memecoins: riskiest
Treating all crypto as one thing is the most common mistake. First, ask which category it is.
The eNaira, launched in October 2021, is issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria. It is not a cryptocurrency.
Stablecoins aim to stay worth 1 US dollar, but the issuer can freeze tokens. In May 2022, TerraUSD lost its dollar value within days.
Established cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ether have long histories, but very large price swings.
NFTs often have little resale demand.
New tokens and memecoins are the riskiest. Many collapse to zero.
Protect your money
Three honest limits
No customer care can reverse a mistake or a scam payment.
A blockchain keeps false data as faithfully as true data.
Check current CBN and SEC Nigeria announcements before you act.
Before you act, know three honest limits. First, payments are final. A mistake or a scam payment usually cannot be undone.
Second, a land record or delivery record on a blockchain is only as true as the person typing the data.
Third, the rules in Nigeria keep changing. The Investments and Securities Act 2025 now treats digital assets as securities under SEC Nigeria.
Always check the CBN and SEC Nigeria websites before acting.
Key points
Remember
A blockchain is a ledger with no single keeper
Each block stores the previous block's hash
Always name the category of asset

To remember. A blockchain is a shared ledger with no single keeper. Each block stores the fingerprint of the one before, so edits show. But tamper-evident does not mean true. Payments are final. And always name the category before you judge it.

Wallets, research and scam defence
Wallets, research and scam defence.
This is the video for module 2 of Blockchain and Digital Assets Literacy.
Why this matters
Your phrase is everything
A wallet holds keys, not coins
Your recovery phrase controls it all
Research before you believe
Know the scams before they find you
Coins do not sit inside your phone. A wallet stores your private key, the secret that lets you sign a payment.
Most wallets make your keys from a recovery phrase of 12 or 24 ordinary words. A stranger with those words does not need your phone, your PIN or your face.
You will learn a research workflow for judging any digital asset.
And you will learn the scams built for crypto, and what to do in the first hour if something goes wrong.
Exchange account or your own wallet
The company holds your keys
Password reset is possible
It can freeze or fail
Identity checks required
You carry all the security
On an exchange, a company holds your keys. It is convenient, but exchanges have failed. FTX collapsed in November 2022, and customers could not withdraw.
In a self-custody wallet, you hold the keys. No company can freeze it, but if you lose or reveal your phrase, nobody can help.
While you are learning, keep only what you are prepared to lose completely.
Safe setup
Setting up a wallet safely
No real support agent will ever ask for your phrase.
Find the official website first
Create it with nobody watching
Write the phrase on paper, in order
Keep two copies in two safe places
Use an authenticator app, not SMS
Step 1. Find the wallet's official website, then follow its own link to the app store. Fake wallet apps copy logos. Never install APK files from WhatsApp.
Step 2. Create the wallet with nobody watching your screen.
Step 3. Write the phrase on paper with a pen. Never photograph it, screenshot it, or save it in notes or on WhatsApp.
Step 4. Make two paper copies and keep them in two separate safe places.
Step 5. On exchanges, use an authenticator app, because SIM swap fraud can steal SMS codes.
Before a big transfer, send a small test first, and check the network and the address.
Anyone who asks you to type your phrase to sync, unlock or claim a reward is stealing it.
Due diligence
Six steps to research any project
A 50% fall needs a 100% rise just to recover.
Write down the claim in one sentence
Read the primary documents
Check the team and the money
Verify on a block explorer
Check SEC Nigeria for warnings
Step 1. Write down the claim, and who gains if you believe it.
Step 2. Read the official website and whitepaper. Why does it need a blockchain at all?
Step 3. Are the founders named and real? How many tokens do insiders own, and when can they sell?
Step 4. Use a block explorer to check the contract address, and whether a few wallets own most of the supply.
Step 5. Search the SEC Nigeria website for warnings.
Step 6. Write a verdict with real potential, real limits and open questions.
And remember the recovery arithmetic. If an asset falls 50%, it must rise 100% to get back.
Know the tell
Three crypto scams to spot
Fake support or a fake sync site asks for your recovery phrase.
Profits grow on screen, then you must pay a fee to withdraw.
A buyer sends a fake bank alert. Check your bank app before you release.
Payments cannot be reversed, so scammers love crypto. The first scam is seed-phrase phishing. The tell is any request for your phrase.
The second is a fake trading platform. The early profit is bait. If you must pay a tax or unlock fee to withdraw, the profits were never real.
The third is P2P payment fraud. Never trust an SMS alert or a screenshot. Open your own bank app and check the naira has landed before you release anything.
Check the maths
Grace tests a 40% monthly promise
For example, Grace is added to a Telegram group promising 40% every month. She has 200,000 naira.
Compounding: multiply by 1.4 each month.
Her savings
After month 1 at 40%
For example, Grace is added to a Telegram group promising 40% every month. She checks the maths first.
She has 200,000 naira. After month 1, that would be 280,000 naira.
Over 12 months, that compounds to about 11,340,000 naira. About 57 times her money in one year.
No honest business delivers that. If it were real, they would not need her 200,000 naira.
The first hour
If you shared your phrase
Fund recovery offers are a second scam.
Make a new wallet on a clean device
Move remaining funds at once
Revoke any bad approvals
Change exchange passwords and 2FA
Save evidence, then report
If you shared your phrase or signed a bad approval, act in this order. First, create a brand-new wallet with a new phrase on a clean device.
Move any remaining funds into it at once.
Revoke any token approval you signed, with a tool such as Revoke.cash.
Change your exchange passwords and two-factor settings.
Then save screenshots and transaction hashes, and report to the exchange, your bank, the police or the EFCC, and SEC Nigeria.
Strangers who promise to trace your crypto for an upfront fee are scammers too.

Once people know you understand blockchain, they will ask you. Your cooperative, your employer, your cousin with a sure token.
You will learn a five-question test for whether a problem really needs a blockchain.
You will learn where education ends and regulated investment advice begins.
And you will build a portfolio that shows balanced understanding.
Listen first
Three kinds of conversation
Ask what they heard and what confuses them. Avoid burying them in jargon.
Could they lose it all? Emergency fund? Does the person who told them earn from it?
What exact problem? Who enters the data? What does the current system cost?
First, work out what kind of conversation you are in. Someone learning needs plain answers, not jargon.
Someone thinking of investing needs questions about her situation. Is this money she could lose completely? Is it for school fees or rent?
Say clearly: I can show you how to check it, but I can't tell you whether to buy.
Someone judging a business use needs questions about the real problem, and what it costs today.
The blockchain test
Does it really need a blockchain?
Mostly no? A simpler tool is almost always better.
Several parties share the records
They do not trust each other
A blockchain is slower and more complex than an ordinary database. It earns its place only when several things are true together. First, do several parties share the records?
Second, do they distrust each other?
Third, is there no acceptable trusted middleman?
Fourth, does tamper-evidence really matter?
Fifth, will the data be entered accurately?
If most answers are no, a simpler tool is almost always better.
Worked example
Folake's cooperative and a blockchain ajo
30 members pay 10,000 naira weekly
Real problem: members can't see records
Only 2 of 5 answers are clearly yes
The app still needs the treasurer's typing
Fix: two-signatory account, shared sheet
For example, Folake chairs a thrift cooperative in Ibadan. 30 members each pay 10,000 naira weekly, so 300,000 naira every week. A vendor offers a blockchain savings app.
The real problem is that members cannot see the records between meetings.
Run the five questions, and only 2 answers are clearly yes.
The app would still depend on the treasurer typing payments correctly, the same as now.
The simpler fix is a bank account needing two signatories, a shared view-only spreadsheet, and the monthly bank statement posted in the WhatsApp group.
Educator, not investment adviser
Needs registration and licence
Stay on the educator side. Explain how things work, teach research and safety, and show scam patterns.
Recommending coins, managing other people's money or promising returns is investment advice. SEC Nigeria regulates this, and it may need registration.
Never collect money to invest for others. Even with good intentions, you can become responsible for their losses.
Honest disclosure
Your rules when you teach
Disclose any asset you own
No payment or free tokens to promote
No buy now signals groups
Say: education, not investment advice
Check SEC Nigeria and CBN for rules
Keep these rules every time. If you own an asset you mention, say so. Never accept money or free tokens to promote a project. Never run buy now alert groups.
Put the line, this is education, not investment advice, on every handout. And check the SEC Nigeria and CBN websites for current rules.
